name: walrus-candidate
summary: An assignment the next `if` test could absorb with `:=`
explanation:
Flags an assignment to a name that only feeds the `if` statement right after it. Inlining the value, or binding it in the test with `:=`, keeps the value next to the check that uses it. ## Why is this bad? A name that exists only to feed the next test splits one decision over two statements. It also stays in scope after it stops mattering. Inlining the value, or binding it in the test with an [assignment expression](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#assignment-expressions) (`:=`, from [PEP 572](https://peps.python.org/pep-0572/)), keeps the value next to the check that uses it. ## Example ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = re.match(r"\w+", text) if found: return found.group(0) stripped = text.strip() if not stripped: return "" return text ``` Use instead: ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: if found := re.match(r"\w+", text): return found.group(0) if not text.strip(): return "" return text ``` ## Configuration - [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python); see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version) ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py37" ``` ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length) and [`indent-width`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#indent-width), which give the width an `if` header must fit; see [Settings shared with Ruff](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#settings-shared-with-ruff) ```toml config [tool.ruff] line-length = 40 ``` ```python ok def check(text: str) -> bool: size = len(text) + len(text) + len(text) + len(text) if size > 1000000: return True return False ``` ## What it does ### Active on An assignment to a single name is reported when it is directly followed by an `if` statement whose test starts with that name, and nothing else reads the name: not after the `if` statement, and not before the assignment either, such as a closure or an earlier statement of the same loop. The search covers the enclosing function, or the whole file at module level. The test starts with the name when the name is: - **The whole test**, as in `if found:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str) -> str: if found := text.strip(): return found return "" ``` - **The operand of `not`**, as in `if not found:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if not found: return "" return text ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str) -> str: if not text.strip(): return "" return text ``` - **The left side of a comparison**, as in `if found > 3:`. ```python report def long_enough(text: str) -> bool: size = len(text) if size > 3: return True return False ``` ```python fixed def long_enough(text: str) -> bool: if len(text) > 3: return True return False ``` - **The first operand of `and` or `or`**, as in `if found and ready:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str, ready: bool) -> str: found = text.strip() if found and ready: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str, ready: bool) -> str: if (found := text.strip()) and ready: return found return "" ``` In each case the value can take the name's place at the start of the test without changing what runs first. ### Exceptions - **Target versions older than 3.8**: Python 3.8 introduced `:=`. ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py37" ``` ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - **Modules with a version gate**, as [missing-final](SMP601.html) describes: the module exists to run on older interpreters and report them. ```python ok import sys if sys.version_info < (3, 8): raise SystemExit("Python 3.8 or newer is required") def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - **Assignments in a class body**, including inside an `if`, `for` or `try` block of the class, unless a function sits between: such an assignment defines a class attribute, which `Class.name` reads without a name reference. ```python ok class Config: found = len("text") if found: LIMIT = found ``` - **Values that are a lambda, `yield`, `yield from`, an `:=` expression or a tuple without parentheses**: these are not reported. ```python ok def run(items: list[str]) -> list[str]: found = lambda: items if found: return found() return items ``` - **Values that mention the name itself**: these are not reported. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() or found if found: return found return text ``` - **Assignments that share a line with other code**: the fix deletes the assignment's whole line. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() other = 1 if found: return found return str(other) ``` - **Assignments with a comment on their line, or between them and the `if`**: deleting the assignment would lose the comment. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() # the stripped text if found: return found return text ``` - **`TYPE_CHECKING`**: type checkers recognize the guard by that name whatever its value, so the name must stay. ```python ok TYPE_CHECKING = False if TYPE_CHECKING: import os ``` - **Module-level names that another module in the run imports or patches by name, or that `__all__` lists, and every module-level name when `__all__` is computed**: the other module would lose the binding. ```python ok file=settings.py found = len("text") if found: print(found) ``` ```python context file=main.py from settings import found ``` - **Names the function declares [`global`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-global-statement) or [`nonlocal`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-nonlocal-statement)**: code in the outer scope reads the binding too. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: global found found = text.strip() if found: return found return text ``` - **An `if` whose header, with the value folded in, would not fit [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length) on one line at its block's indentation**: `ruff format` would split it over several lines, which reads worse than the two statements. The header is measured joined on one line without parentheses around the test, which the formatter drops, so how the code is laid out now does not matter. A header with a comment or a string over several lines never fits. ```python ok def run(text: str, flag: bool) -> str: found = text.strip() if flag and found and text.startswith("a") and text.endswith("b") and text.isalpha() and text.isascii(): return found return text ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD assign["name = value"] --> test{"next if test
starts with name?"} test -->|no| skip["not reported"] test -->|yes| read{"name read
anywhere else?"} read -->|yes| skip read -->|no| skipped{"skipped case, or
header too long?"} skipped -->|yes| skip skipped -->|no| again{"name used again
in the if?"} again -->|yes| walrus["fix: name := value
in the test"] again -->|no| inline["fix: inline the value"] classDef blue fill:#9cc0e3,stroke:#1f4f7d,color:#062d59 classDef yellow fill:#f2d27a,stroke:#6b5410,color:#062d59 classDef green fill:#93cfa9,stroke:#1d5e3a,color:#0b2e1a classDef teal fill:#8ccbc3,stroke:#145c55,color:#072b28 classDef orange fill:#f0b48c,stroke:#8a3d12,color:#3d1606 class assign blue class test,read,skipped,again yellow class skip green class walrus,inline teal ``` ### Fix The fix is safe. It deletes the assignment, then: - when the name appears nowhere else in the `if` statement, including the rest of the test, the body and any `elif` or `else` branch, it inlines the value and adds parentheses where precedence requires them; ```python report def run(text: str) -> bool: found = text.strip() + "!" if found: return True return False ``` ```python fixed def run(text: str) -> bool: if text.strip() + "!": return True return False ``` - otherwise it writes `name := value` in the test, in parentheses unless the name is the whole test. ```python report def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def run(text: str) -> str: if found := text.strip(): return found return "" ``` The search for other reads looks only at names in code. It misses importers outside the run and references held in strings, such as an `__all__` entry.

name: string-concatenation
summary: `+` between strings
explanation:
Flags `+` chains that join a string literal or f-string with other values. An f-string shows the final text in one piece, where a `+` chain scatters it across quotes and operators. ## Why is this bad? A chain of `+` scatters the text across quotes and operators, and every non-string operand needs an explicit `str()`. An f-string ([PEP 498](https://peps.python.org/pep-0498/)) shows the final text in one piece. ## Example ```python report message = "Hello, " + name + "!" ``` Use instead: ```python ok message = f"Hello, {name}!" ``` ## Configuration - [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python); see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version) ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311" ``` ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.strip('"') + "!" ``` ## What it does ### Active on - **`+` chains that join a string literal or [f-string](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#f-strings) with other values**, such as `"Hello, " + name + "!"`: the whole chain is reported once. **Unsafe fix:** always, and offered only when the code shows every operand is a `str`. `+` raises [`TypeError`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#TypeError) for a non-string operand and honors a custom [`__add__`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__add__) or `__radd__`, such as `markupsafe.Markup` escaping the other operand, while an f-string formats any value. ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name + "!" ``` ```python fixed def greet(name: str) -> str: return f"Hello, {name}!" ``` ### Exceptions - **Chains that contain a bytes literal**: Python has no bytes f-string to write them as. ```python ok def header(name: bytes) -> bytes: return b"Name: " + name ``` ### Deciding on a fix ```mermaid flowchart TD chain["+ chain with a string"] --> bytes{"holds a
bytes literal?"} bytes -->|yes| skip["not reported"] bytes -->|no| known{"every operand
known str?"} known -->|no| none["reported, no fix"] known -->|yes| fits{"chain fits
an f-string?"} fits -->|no| none fits -->|yes| fix["reported,
unsafe fix"] classDef blue fill:#9cc0e3,stroke:#1f4f7d,color:#062d59 classDef yellow fill:#f2d27a,stroke:#6b5410,color:#062d59 classDef green fill:#93cfa9,stroke:#1d5e3a,color:#0b2e1a classDef teal fill:#8ccbc3,stroke:#145c55,color:#072b28 classDef orange fill:#f0b48c,stroke:#8a3d12,color:#3d1606 class chain blue class bytes,known,fits yellow class skip green class none orange class fix teal ``` ### Known `str` operands An operand is known to be a `str` when it is one of these. Literals and expressions: - a string literal or f-string, `"..." % values`, or a `str` repeated by an `int`, such as `"-" * width` - an index or slice of a `str`, or an item of a list, tuple, set or mapping of them, such as `name.split(".")[0]` or `names[0]` for `names: list[str]` - a conditional between `str` values, or `a or "default"` where `a` is a `str` or `None` Builtins and the standard library: - a call to the builtin `str`, `repr`, `ascii`, `format`, `chr`, `hex`, `oct` or `bin` - a `str` method such as `join`, `format` or `upper` called on a `str`, or `decode` on `bytes` - `__name__`, `__qualname__` and `__module__` of anything, and the module's `__name__` and `__file__` - standard library values the module imports: `os.sep`, `os.linesep`, `sys.platform`, the `string` constants, `os.getcwd()`, `platform.system()`, `json.dumps(...)`, `textwrap.dedent(...)`, `os.environ[...]`, `os.environ.get(key, "default")`, `os.getenv(key, "default")`, `uuid.uuid4().hex`, `os.path.join(...)` and the other `os.path` functions given a `str`, and the `name`, `stem`, `suffix` and `as_posix()` of a `pathlib.Path` Code of the module: - a call to a function or method of the module annotated `-> str`, undecorated or with `functools.cache` - an attribute of an instance of a class of the module that annotates it `str`, or a property annotated `-> str` - on `self`, also an attribute that the class body and its methods only ever set to such values, when nothing else writes it and no subclass may override it - a name every binding of which, in the scope it resolves to, gives such a value: an assignment, a loop over such items, a `with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path`, or an annotation `str` (also `Final[str]`, `Annotated[str, ...]`) that no binding contradicts A name that an unannotated parameter, an import, a `global` or a type parameter binds is not known, so `value + "!"` for an unannotated `value` is reported without a fix. The annotations are trusted: a parameter annotated `str` can still receive a `str` subclass with its own `__add__`. ### Fix The fix copies each non-literal operand into a placeholder as written: - A call to the builtin `str`, `repr` or `ascii` becomes the matching conversion, as Ruff's [explicit-f-string-type-conversion](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/explicit-f-string-type-conversion/) asks, so `"n=" + str(n)` becomes `f"n={n!s}"`. ```python report def label(n: int) -> str: return "n=" + str(n) ``` ```python fixed def label(n: int) -> str: return f"n={n!s}" ``` - A generator passed bare to `str`, `repr` or `ascii` gets parentheses of its own, since a replacement field takes only a yield or star expression unparenthesized. ```python report def label(values: list[int]) -> str: return "values=" + str(value for value in values) ``` ```python fixed def label(values: list[int]) -> str: return f"values={(value for value in values)!s}" ``` - A chain of plain string literals becomes one plain string. ```python report def title() -> str: return "Hello, " + "world" ``` ```python fixed def title() -> str: return "Hello, world" ``` No fix is offered when: - a literal is implicitly concatenated, triple-quoted, raw or `u`-prefixed; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name ``` - the literals use different quote characters; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name + "!" ``` - a comment sits between the operands, since the f-string has no place for it; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return ( "Hello, " # the greeting + name ) ``` - a non-literal operand spans several lines or contains a backslash, `#`, `:`, `!`, `{` or `}`; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.replace(":", "") + "!" ``` - a name is bound by a [PEP 695](https://peps.python.org/pep-0695/) type parameter of the enclosing function or class, as its kind is not known; ```toml config [project] requires-python = ">=3.12" ``` ```python report s = "x" def f[s]() -> str: return "a" + s ``` - the target Python version is older than 3.12 and a non-literal operand contains the string's quote character, which f-strings allow only from 3.12 on ([PEP 701](https://peps.python.org/pep-0701/#considerations-of-quote-reuse)). ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311" ``` ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.strip('"') + "!" ```

name: single-use-variable
summary: Variables read once, right below their assignment
explanation:
Flags a local variable that is assigned once and read once, in the statement right after the assignment. Inlining its
value removes the name and keeps the value next to the code that uses it.

## Why is this bad?

A name that exists only to be read on the next line adds a step to follow without adding meaning. The reader has to find
the assignment, remember the value, and then reach the line that uses it. Inlining the value keeps the decision in one
place.

## Example

```python report
def total_price(prices: list[float]) -> str:
    total = sum(prices)
    return f"{total:.2f}"
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def total_price(prices: list[float]) -> str:
    return f"{sum(prices):.2f}"
```

## Configuration

- [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length) and
  [`indent-width`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#indent-width), which give the width a statement must fit after
  the value is inlined; see
  [Settings shared with Ruff](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#settings-shared-with-ruff)

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python),
  which decide the f-strings that cannot hold a backslash or their own quote before Python 3.12, and the decorators that
  must be dotted names before Python 3.9; see
  [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff]
  target-version = "py312"
  ```

  ```python report
  def quote(value: str) -> str:
      quoted = value.replace("'", "''")
      return f"'{quoted}'"
  ```

## What it does

### Active on

- **A plain assignment to one name whose only other mention is the next statement's read**: the name is bound once in
  the function, and read once, in the statement directly after the assignment, in the same block.

  ```python report
  def price(prices: list[float]) -> str:
      total = sum(prices)
      return f"{total:.2f}"


  def show(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(count)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def price(prices: list[float]) -> str:
      return f"{sum(prices):.2f}"


  def show(items: list[str]) -> None:
      print(len(items))
  ```

- **A dict or set display inlined right after an f-string field's `{`**: the value gets a space inside the braces,
  because `{{` would be read as an escaped brace.

  ```python report
  def show(key: str) -> None:
      mapping = {key: 2}
      print(f"{mapping}")
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def show(key: str) -> None:
      print(f"{ {key: 2} }")
  ```

- **A read in an f-string field with a [`=`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#f-strings) debug
  specifier**, such as `{total=}`: the field prints the text of its expression, so the text stays as written and the
  value moves into a plain field after it. The printed text does not change.

  ```python report
  def show(items: list[str]) -> None:
      total = len(items)
      print(f"{total=}")
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def show(items: list[str]) -> None:
      print(f"total={len(items)!r}")
  ```

- **Before Python 3.12, a value whose strings use the f-string's quote**: a string in the value takes the other quote,
  which the field can hold.

  ```python report
  def join(items: list[str]) -> str:
      sep = " ".join(items)
      return f"[{sep}]"
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def join(items: list[str]) -> str:
      return f"[{' '.join(items)}]"
  ```

### Exceptions

- **A name that is `_`, or a dunder such as `__all__`**: `_` is a placeholder, and a dunder has a meaning to Python.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      _ = len(items)
      print(_)
  ```

- **A name the function declares [`global`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-global-statement)
  or [`nonlocal`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-nonlocal-statement)**: code outside the
  function reads the binding too.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      global count
      count = len(items)
      print(count)
  ```

- **A value that is a `yield`, `await` or `:=` expression**: these run or bind in a way that moving them changes.

  ```python ok
  async def run(source: Source) -> None:
      data = await source.read()
      print(data)
  ```

- **A next statement that is `return name` or `yield name`**: Ruff's
  [unnecessary-assign](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unnecessary-assign/) covers the `return` case, and `yield`
  keeps the same shape.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> int:
      count = len(items)
      return count
  ```

- **A read inside a loop body, a comprehension, a lambda or a nested function**: inlining would compute the value once
  per pass instead of once.

  ```python ok
  def run(rows: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
      total = sum(rows[0])
      return [total + value for value in rows[1]]
  ```

- **A read in a nested block of the next statement**, such as the body of an `if`: the value would run only when the
  block does, so inlining would skip it when the block is not taken.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str], verbose: bool) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      if verbose:
          print(count)
  ```

- **A read after `and` or `or`**, or in a branch of a conditional expression, a later link of a chained comparison, an
  `assert`, a `case` or the type of an `except` clause: each runs only when the code before it does not decide the
  outcome, or when an exception or a match reaches it.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str], flag: bool) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(flag and count)
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str], flag: bool) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(count if flag else 0)
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str], low: int) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(low < 0 < count)
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      assert count, "no items"
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(command: str, items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      match command:
          case "count":
              print(count)
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      error = ValueError
      try:
          print(items[0])
      except error:
          print("empty")
  ```

- **A read in an annotation, a `type` statement or a type parameter**: an annotation in a function body is never
  evaluated, and the others are evaluated lazily, so the value would not run where the name was read.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      kind = list[str]
      values: kind = items
      print(values)
  ```

- **Before Python 3.12, a value with a backslash, or whose strings hold the other quote**: a replacement field cannot
  hold a backslash or the f-string's own quote until [PEP 701](https://peps.python.org/pep-0701/), and a string that
  holds the other quote cannot take it, so the inlined code would not parse.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff]
  target-version = "py311"
  ```

  ```python ok
  def quote(value: str) -> str:
      quoted = value.replace("'", "''")
      return f"'{quoted}'"
  ```

- **An assignment with a comment on its line, or between it and the read**: inlining would lose the comment.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)  # the number of rows
      print(count)
  ```

- **A name read in an `if` test that starts with it**: [walrus-candidate](SMP502.html) covers those, and writes the
  value into the test.

  ```python ok
  def run(text: str) -> None:
      found = text.find("x")
      if found:
          print(found)
  ```

- **A name read again elsewhere in the function**, or bound again: the name is needed after the read, or the read is not
  the only one.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(count)
      print(count)
  ```

- **Functions that read their locals by name, such as `locals()` or `eval`**: a removed name would vanish from what they
  see.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      print(locals())
  ```

- **A next statement that is a `while` loop**: its test runs again on every pass.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      limit = len(items)
      while limit:
          limit -= 1
  ```

- **An inlined header that would no longer fit [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length)**:
  `ruff format` would split the statement over several lines, which reads worse than the two statements. The header is
  measured joined on one line at its block's indentation, with the value in place of the name.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff]
  line-length = 40
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items) + len(items) + len(items)
      print(count + 1000000)
  ```

- **A message bound for an exception call in a `raise`**: Ruff's
  [raw-string-in-exception](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/raw-string-in-exception/) and
  [f-string-in-exception](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/f-string-in-exception/) ask for an exception's message to be
  a variable, so inlining it would bring back the report those rules remove.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      msg = f"{len(items)} items"
      raise ValueError(msg)
  ```

- **A name bound another way in the function**, such as by an `import`, a `def`, a `class`, an `except` clause or a
  `match` capture: the other binding is a second assignment the walk does not follow, so the name is not single-use.

  ```python ok
  def run(items: list[str]) -> None:
      count = len(items)
      from os import count

      print(count)
  ```

### Fix

The fix deletes the assignment and writes the value where the name was, in parentheses when its precedence requires
them.

**Unsafe fix:** the next statement calls something, awaits, or reads an attribute or a subscript before the read, so the
value would run after it instead of before.

```python report
def run(items: list[str], log: Log) -> None:
    count = len(items)
    log.write(count)
```

```python fixed
def run(items: list[str], log: Log) -> None:
    log.write(len(items))
```

Here `log.write` is looked up before `len(items)` runs, which differs only when that lookup has side effects.

name: single-caller-helper
summary: Private helpers with one short call site, which inlining would keep short

name: unused-default
summary: Parameter defaults that every call passes explicitly
explanation:
Flags a parameter default that every call of the function in the run passes explicitly, by position or by keyword.

## Why is this bad?

A default that no call relies on documents a value nobody uses. A reader looks at the signature to learn what the
function falls back to, and the fallback misleads once every caller supplies its own value.

## Example

```python report
def connect(host, timeout=30):
    return host, timeout


connect("db", 5)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def connect(host, timeout):
    return host, timeout


connect("db", 5)
```

## Configuration

- [`project-kind`](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#library-or-application): a
  library's public functions are left alone, since code outside the project may call them without the argument.

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint]
  project-kind = "application"
  ```

  ```python report
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout


  connect("db", 5)
  ```

## What it does

Calls are counted across the whole run, with names resolved through imports. A call that passes an argument for a
parameter by position counts for it, and so does one that passes it by keyword.

### Active on

- **Module-level functions called in the run**: each call in the defining file, and each call from another file that
  imports the function through its module.

  ```python report
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout


  connect("db", 5)
  connect("cache", timeout=2)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def connect(host, timeout):
      return host, timeout


  connect("db", 5)
  connect("cache", timeout=2)
  ```

- **Keyword-only parameters**: a parameter after `*` is passed by keyword only, so every call names it.

  ```python report
  def retry(count, *, delay=1):
      return count, delay


  retry(3, delay=2)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def retry(count, *, delay):
      return count, delay


  retry(3, delay=2)
  ```

- **Calls from other files**: the calls of a function count wherever they are, so a default is reported only when no
  file in the run leaves it out.

  ```python report file=lib/core.py
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout
  ```

  ```python context file=app/main.py
  from lib.core import connect


  connect("db", 5)
  ```

- **Methods called through `self`**: a method of a module-level class without bases, when the run reads its name only as
  `self.name(...)` calls inside that class. Another `obj.name` read anywhere in the run, or a subclass of the class,
  leaves the method alone, since the rule cannot tell which receiver it is.

  ```python report
  class Client:
      def send(self, data, flush=False):
          return data, flush

      def push(self, data):
          return self.send(data, True)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  class Client:
      def send(self, data, flush):
          return data, flush

      def push(self, data):
          return self.send(data, True)
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Functions with no call in the run**: there is nothing to pass the default, so the rule has no evidence either way.

  ```python ok
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout
  ```

- **Calls that unpack `*args` or `**kwargs`**: the unpacked values can supply any parameter.

  - `*args`: the call unpacks a sequence into positional arguments.

    ```python ok
    def connect(host, timeout=30):
        return host, timeout


    connect("db", *extra)
    connect("db", 5)
    ```

  - `**kwargs`: the call unpacks a mapping into keyword arguments.

    ```python ok
    def connect(host, timeout=30):
        return host, timeout


    connect("db", **options)
    connect("db", 5)
    ```

- **Functions used other than as a call**: passed as a value, registered by a decorator, or named by a dotted string or
  an entry point, where the calls that reach it are not all visible.

  ```python ok
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout


  connect("db", 5)
  handlers = [connect]
  ```

- **Decorated functions**: a decorator may register or wrap the function, so its calls may not be the ones written.

  ```python ok
  from functools import lru_cache


  @lru_cache
  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout


  connect("db", 5)
  ```

- **Dunder methods**: `__init__` and the other dunders are called by Python itself, not by name.

  ```python ok
  class Client:
      def __init__(self, timeout=30):
          self.timeout = timeout


  Client(5)
  ```

- **Public functions of a library**: outside code may call them without the argument.

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint]
  project-kind = "library"
  api-modules = ["lib.core"]
  ```

  ```python ok file=lib/core.py
  __all__ = ["connect"]


  def connect(host, timeout=30):
      return host, timeout
  ```

  ```python context file=app/main.py
  from lib.core import connect


  connect("db", 5)
  ```

- **Methods of classes with bases, or whose name is read elsewhere**: the calls of a method through `self` may be
  overridden in a subclass, or the name may be read through another object.

  ```python ok
  class Base:
      pass


  class Client(Base):
      def send(self, data, flush=False):
          return data, flush

      def push(self, data):
          return self.send(data, True)
  ```

### Fix

The fix deletes the default, from its `=` to the end of its value. It is offered only when the signature stays valid: a
keyword-only parameter always qualifies, and a positional one only when no parameter before it has a default. Removing
the default of `first` in `def pair(first=1, second=2)` lets `second` qualify on the next pass, so the fixed output
below drops both.

**Unsafe fix:** the fix relies on the calls the run shows, so a call from outside the run may break.

```python report
def pair(first=1, second=2):
    return first, second


pair(1, 2)
```

```python fixed
def pair(first, second):
    return first, second


pair(1, 2)
```

name: up-comprehension-unpacking
summary: Nested `for` clauses that only unpack their iterable into the element
explanation:
Flags a nested `for` clause that only unpacks its iterable, and moves the unpacking into the element, which Python 3.15
allows.

## Why is this bad?

A second `for` clause that does nothing but unpack the outer item takes a loop to say what the element can say in one
place. [PEP 798](https://peps.python.org/pep-0798/) lets the element unpack with `*` for lists, sets and generators, and
with `**` for dicts.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
flat = [x for group in groups for x in group]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
flat = [*group for group in groups]
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
  flat = [x for group in groups for x in group]
  ```

## What it does

Reports a list, set or generator comprehension with exactly two `for` clauses, or a dict comprehension whose inner
clause unpacks `.items()`, when:

- the outer clause binds a name, `group` here, and the inner clause iterates that name, with no `if` clause and no
  `async` in either.
- the element is the inner clause's target, a name other than `group`. For a dict, the key and value are the two names
  of the inner target.

### Active on

The list, set and generator comprehensions, which unpack with `*`:

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
flat_set = {x for group in groups for x in group}
flat_gen = (x for group in groups for x in group)
```

```python fixed
groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
flat_set = {*group for group in groups}
flat_gen = (*group for group in groups)
```

The dict comprehensions, which unpack with `**`:

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
pairs = [{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}]
merged = {key: value for entry in pairs for key, value in entry.items()}
```

```python fixed
pairs = [{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}]
merged = {**entry for entry in pairs}
```

### Exceptions

- **A comprehension with an `if` clause or `async`**: the clauses no longer read as one unpacking.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
  flat = [x for group in groups for x in group if x]
  ```

- **An inner iterable other than the outer name**: the element comes from another source.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
  other = [[4]]
  flat = [x for group in groups for x in other]
  ```

- **A dict over `.keys()`, or with a call that takes arguments**: the pairs do not come from `.items()` alone.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  pairs = [{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}]
  keys = {key: value for entry in pairs for key, value in entry.keys()}
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.15**: the syntax is a `SyntaxError` there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  groups = [[1, 2], [3]]
  flat = [x for group in groups for x in group]
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe for lists, sets and generators. It rewrites the element and removes the inner `for` clause. The fix for
a dict is unsafe: `**` reads `keys()` and `__getitem__`, not `items()`, so the rewrite needs a real `dict`.

name: up-traceback-exception-arguments
summary: `traceback` calls that pass an exception's type and traceback next to it
explanation:
Flags `traceback` calls that pass an exception's type and traceback next to the exception, which Python 3.10 reads from
the exception itself.

## Why is this bad?

Since Python 3.10 the `traceback` functions take the exception alone, and read its type and traceback from it. The
three-argument form repeats what the exception already carries, and makes the call longer to read.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.10"
```

```python report
import traceback


def report(run):
    try:
        run()
    except Exception as error:
        traceback.print_exception(type(error), error, error.__traceback__)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import traceback


def report(run):
    try:
        run()
    except Exception as error:
        traceback.print_exception(error)
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.9"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import traceback


  def report(run):
      try:
          run()
      except Exception as error:
          traceback.print_exception(type(error), error, error.__traceback__)
  ```

## What it does

Reports a call that resolves to `traceback.print_exception`, `traceback.format_exception` or
`traceback.format_exception_only` and passes:

- **Three positional arguments** to the first two functions: `type(error)` or `error.__class__`, then `error`, then
  `error.__traceback__`, all for the same name.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import traceback


  def report(error):
      return traceback.format_exception(error.__class__, error, error.__traceback__, limit=2)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import traceback


  def report(error):
      return traceback.format_exception(error, limit=2)
  ```

- **Two positional arguments** to `format_exception_only`: `type(error)`, then `error`.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import traceback


  def report(error):
      return traceback.format_exception_only(type(error), error)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import traceback


  def report(error):
      return traceback.format_exception_only(error)
  ```

### Exceptions

- **A traceback that is not the exception's own**: the call passes a different traceback, which the exception does not
  carry.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import traceback


  def report(error, saved):
      return traceback.format_exception(type(error), error, saved)
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.10**: the single-argument form raises `TypeError` there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.9"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import traceback


  def report(error):
      return traceback.format_exception(type(error), error, error.__traceback__)
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe. It replaces the first arguments with the exception and keeps the keyword arguments, such as `limit=`
and `chain=`.

name: up-exc-info-exception
summary: `sys.exc_info()` reads of the exception being handled
explanation:
Flags `sys.exc_info()` reads of the exception being handled, which `sys.exception()` returns directly from Python 3.11.

## Why is this bad?

`sys.exc_info()` returns a tuple of three values, and code that reads its second value, or unpacks all three into
`traceback.print_exception`, only needs the exception. `sys.exception()` names that value and returns it alone.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

```python report
import sys

error = sys.exc_info()[1]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import sys

error = sys.exception()
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import sys

  error = sys.exc_info()[1]
  ```

## What it does

Reports these forms, when the call resolves to `sys.exc_info`, so `import sys as system` counts:

- **`sys.exc_info()[1]`**: a read of the second value.
- **`traceback.print_exception(*sys.exc_info())`**: an unpacking of the whole tuple as the only argument.

### Exceptions

- **The first or third value**: `sys.exc_info()[0]` and `sys.exc_info()[2]` have no single call with the same result.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.11"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import sys

  kind = sys.exc_info()[0]
  trace = sys.exc_info()[2]
  ```

- **A call imported by name**: `from sys import exc_info` gives a call the rule does not rewrite.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.11"
  ```

  ```python ok
  from sys import exc_info

  error = exc_info()[1]
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.11**: `sys.exception()` does not exist there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import sys

  error = sys.exc_info()[1]
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe. It replaces the subscript with `sys.exception()`, or the unpacked argument with it, which gives the
same value.

name: up-object-sentinel
summary: `object()` placeholders `sentinel` would name
explanation:
Flags a module or class constant assigned a bare `object()` placeholder, which `sentinel` from Python 3.15 names.

## Why is this bad?

A bare `object()` reprs as an address, so a traceback or a debugger shows `<object object at 0x7f...>` where the name
would tell the reader which placeholder it is. `sentinel` takes the name and uses it in the repr.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
_MISSING = object()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
_MISSING = sentinel("_MISSING")
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  _MISSING = object()
  ```

## What it does

Reports a single-name assignment of a bare `object()` call, with no arguments, when it sits in a module body or a class
body and the name is assigned only once in the file.

### Active on

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
class Config:
    SENTINEL = object()
```

```python fixed
class Config:
    SENTINEL = sentinel("SENTINEL")
```

### Exceptions

- **A name assigned again**: the second binding is a different object, so the placeholder is not the only one.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  _MISSING = object()
  _MISSING = 2
  ```

- **A placeholder in a function**: a local is not visible by name outside the function.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  def run():
      missing = object()
      return missing
  ```

- **A file that already spells `sentinel`**: the name may be a different binding.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  sentinel = 1
  _MISSING = object()
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.15**: the builtin does not exist there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  _MISSING = object()
  ```

### Fix

The fix is unsafe. The repr changes from an address to the name, which a program can read, and a pickled `sentinel`
loads only when the module has an attribute of the same name, so the name must match the module attribute the value is
stored under.

name: up-context-var-token-reset
summary: `ContextVar.set()` tokens reset in a `finally` block
explanation:
Flags a `ContextVar.set()` token that a `try` block resets in its `finally` clause, which a `with` block does on exit
from Python 3.14.

## Why is this bad?

Since Python 3.14 the token `ContextVar.set()` returns is a context manager that resets the variable when the block
ends. The `try`/`finally` pair repeats that by hand, and leaves a name in scope that nothing else reads.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
```

```python report
import contextvars

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")


def handle(value):
    token = request_id.set(value)
    try:
        return process()
    finally:
        request_id.reset(token)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import contextvars

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")


def handle(value):
    with request_id.set(value):
        return process()
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.13"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import contextvars

  request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")


  def handle(value):
      token = request_id.set(value)
      try:
          return process()
      finally:
          request_id.reset(token)
  ```

## What it does

Reports an assignment `token = variable.set(value)` followed directly by a `try` whose only clause is a `finally` that
holds `variable.reset(token)`, with no `except` and no `else`.

### Active on

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
```

```python report
import contextvars

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
token = request_id.set("one")
try:
    print(request_id.get())
finally:
    request_id.reset(token)
```

```python fixed
import contextvars

request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
with request_id.set("one"):
    print(request_id.get())
```

### Exceptions

- **A token read outside the reset**: the block would take the name's last use away.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import contextvars

  request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
  token = request_id.set("one")
  try:
      print(request_id.get())
  finally:
      request_id.reset(token)
  print(token)
  ```

- **A `finally` with more than the reset**: the statements after the reset would run inside the block.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import contextvars

  request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
  token = request_id.set("one")
  try:
      print(request_id.get())
  finally:
      request_id.reset(token)
      print("done")
  ```

- **A reset on another variable**: the token belongs to the variable it was set on.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import contextvars

  request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
  user = contextvars.ContextVar("user")
  token = request_id.set("one")
  try:
      print(request_id.get())
  finally:
      user.reset(token)
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.14**: the token is not a context manager there, and `with` raises `TypeError`.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.13"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import contextvars

  request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id")
  token = request_id.set("one")
  try:
      print(request_id.get())
  finally:
      request_id.reset(token)
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe and reports without a fix when a comment sits in the lines it would remove, which would lose the
comment.

name: up-chdir-restore
summary: Working directories restored in a `finally` block
explanation:
Flags a directory change that a `try` block undoes in its `finally` clause, which `contextlib.chdir` does from Python
3.11.

## Why is this bad?

Saving the working directory, changing it and restoring it in a `finally` clause takes three statements and a `try`,
where `contextlib.chdir` needs one `with` block. The block also cannot forget the restore.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

```python report
import os


def build(target):
    old = os.getcwd()
    os.chdir(target)
    try:
        return compile_project()
    finally:
        os.chdir(old)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import contextlib


def build(target):
    with contextlib.chdir(target):
        return compile_project()
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import os


  def build(target):
      old = os.getcwd()
      os.chdir(target)
      try:
          return compile_project()
      finally:
          os.chdir(old)
  ```

## What it does

Reports three statements in one body: `old = os.getcwd()`, then `os.chdir(target)` with one argument, then a `try` whose
only clause is a `finally` that holds `os.chdir(old)`, with no `except` and no `else`. The name `old` must appear
nowhere else in its function, or in the module at module level.

### Active on

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

```python report
import os


def run(target):
    old = os.getcwd()
    os.chdir(target)
    try:
        step()
    finally:
        os.chdir(old)
```

```python fixed
import contextlib


def run(target):
    with contextlib.chdir(target):
        step()
```

### Exceptions

- **The saved directory read after the block**: the name has another use.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.11"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import os


  def run(target):
      old = os.getcwd()
      os.chdir(target)
      try:
          step()
      finally:
          os.chdir(old)
      print(old)
  ```

- **A `finally` that changes the directory to another place**: the restore does not return to the saved directory.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.11"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import os


  def run(target):
      old = os.getcwd()
      os.chdir(target)
      try:
          step()
      finally:
          os.chdir(target)
  ```

- **Target versions before 3.11**: `contextlib.chdir` does not exist there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import os


  def run(target):
      old = os.getcwd()
      os.chdir(target)
      try:
          step()
      finally:
          os.chdir(old)
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe under those conditions. It adds `import contextlib` before the module's first import, unless the module
imports `contextlib` already. When another binding holds the name `contextlib`, the rule reports without a fix. It also
reports without a fix when a comment sits in the lines it would remove.

name: up-strptime-date
summary: `datetime.strptime()` results narrowed to a `date` or `time`
explanation:
Flags `datetime.strptime(...).date()` and `datetime.strptime(...).time()`, which Python 3.14 replaces with
`date.strptime` and `time.strptime`.

## Why is this bad?

`datetime.strptime(text, format).date()` builds a full datetime to keep one part of it. From Python 3.14 `date` and
`time` parse their own part, which says what the code reads and skips the intermediate value.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
```

```python report
from datetime import datetime


def parse_day(text):
    return datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
from datetime import date


def parse_day(text):
    return date.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d")
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.13"
  ```

  ```python ok
  from datetime import datetime


  def parse_day(text):
      return datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
  ```

## What it does

Reports a call `.date()` or `.time()` with no arguments on a call that resolves to `datetime.datetime.strptime`, whether
the class is imported by name or reached through the `datetime` module.

### Active on

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
```

```python report
import datetime


def parse_day(text):
    return datetime.datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
```

```python fixed
import datetime


def parse_day(text):
    return datetime.date.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d")
```

### Exceptions

- **Target versions before 3.14**: `date.strptime` does not exist there.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.13"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import datetime


  def parse_day(text):
      return datetime.datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe for `.date()`. For `.time()` it is safe when the format is a string literal without `%z`, and unsafe
otherwise: `time.strptime` keeps the zone that `.time()` drops, so the value changes with `%z`. When the class is
imported by name, the fix adds `date` or `time` to that `from datetime import` line. It reports without a fix when the
file already spells `date` or `time` outside an attribute, since the new name would take that binding's place.

name: up-event-loop-in-coroutine
summary: `asyncio.get_event_loop()` calls in coroutines
explanation:
Flags `asyncio.get_event_loop()` calls inside coroutines, where `asyncio.get_running_loop()` returns the loop the
coroutine runs on.

## Why is this bad?

A coroutine runs on a loop that is always running, so `get_event_loop()` only has to return that loop.
`get_running_loop()` returns it directly and raises `RuntimeError` when no loop runs, which surfaces a mistake that
`get_event_loop()` would hide. `get_event_loop()` also serves code outside a loop, where Python 3.10 deprecated the
implicit loop creation and Python 3.14 made the call raise `RuntimeError`.

## Example

```python report
import asyncio


async def run() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
    return asyncio.get_event_loop()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import asyncio


async def run() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
    return asyncio.get_running_loop()
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **`asyncio.get_event_loop()` with no arguments, called inside an `async def`**: a class body inside the coroutine
  counts as part of it, while a nested `def` or `lambda` does not. **Safe fix:** the attribute is renamed to
  `get_running_loop`. A call through a name imported from `asyncio`, such as `get_event_loop()`, is reported without a
  fix.

  ```python report
  import asyncio


  async def run() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
      return asyncio.get_event_loop()
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import asyncio


  async def run() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
      return asyncio.get_running_loop()
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Calls in plain functions**: such a function may run before any loop starts, where `get_running_loop()` raises.

  ```python ok
  import asyncio


  def start() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
      return asyncio.get_event_loop()
  ```

- **Calls in a nested `def` or `lambda` of a coroutine**: the nested function may run after the loop stops.

  ```python ok
  import asyncio


  async def run():
      def later() -> asyncio.AbstractEventLoop:
          return asyncio.get_event_loop()

      return later
  ```

name: up-asyncio-iscoroutinefunction
summary: `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction()` calls
explanation:
Flags `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction()` calls, which `inspect.iscoroutinefunction()` replaces.

## Why is this bad?

Python 3.14 deprecates `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction()`. It also accepts functions marked with the `_is_coroutine` marker
that the `asyncio.coroutine` decorator set, a decorator removed in Python 3.11. `inspect.iscoroutinefunction()` checks
only the function itself, so the two answer differently for such functions.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.10"
```

```python report
import asyncio


async def run(task):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    if asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(task):
        return await task()
    return task()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import asyncio
import inspect


async def run(task):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(task):
        return await task()
    return task()
```

## Configuration

No setting changes the report. Every target version has `inspect.iscoroutinefunction()`, so the rule reports on every
target.

## What it does

### Active on

- **Calls of `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction`**, by its qualified name or by a name imported from `asyncio`. **Unsafe
  fix:** the call becomes `inspect.iscoroutinefunction(...)`, which changes the answer for a function marked with the
  legacy `_is_coroutine` marker. The fix adds `import inspect` when the module does not import it yet.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import asyncio


  async def run(task):
      await asyncio.sleep(0)
      if asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(task):
          return await task()
      return task()
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import asyncio
  import inspect


  async def run(task):
      await asyncio.sleep(0)
      if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(task):
          return await task()
      return task()
  ```

### Fix

The import goes before the first top-level import that sorts after `inspect`, or after the last top-level import. No fix
is offered when:

- `inspect` is already bound to something else in the module, which the import would shadow;

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import asyncio
  from tools import inspect


  def check(task):
      return asyncio.iscoroutinefunction(task)
  ```

name: up-codecs-open
summary: `codecs.open()` calls
explanation:
Flags `codecs.open()` calls, which the builtin `open()` replaces.

## Why is this bad?

Python 3.14 deprecates `codecs.open()`, and the builtin `open()` takes the same arguments. With an encoding,
`codecs.open()` opens the file in binary mode and decodes it through a stream wrapper. That wrapper splits lines at the
characters `str.splitlines()` honors, such as form feeds and U+2028, where `open()` splits only at line endings. With
`newline=""`, `open()` also keeps the line endings as they are, as `codecs.open()` does.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.10"
```

```python report
import codecs


def read_config(path):
    with codecs.open(path, "r", "utf-8") as handle:
        return handle.read()


def encoding_name():
    return codecs.lookup("utf-8").name
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import codecs


def read_config(path):
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
        return handle.read()


def encoding_name():
    return codecs.lookup("utf-8").name
```

## Configuration

No setting changes the report. The rule reports on every target version, since `open()` takes the arguments in each of
them.

## What it does

### Active on

- **Calls of `codecs.open`**, by its qualified name or by a name imported from `codecs`. **Unsafe fix:** the call
  becomes `open(...)` with `encoding=` and `newline=""`. Reading and writing whole files give the same text and bytes,
  but iterating over lines does not for text with a form feed, U+2028, U+001C or U+0085: `codecs.open()` yields a line
  at each of them, and `open()` does not.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import codecs


  def read_config(path):
      with codecs.open(path, "r", "utf-8") as handle:
          return handle.read()


  def encoding_name():
      return codecs.lookup("utf-8").name
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import codecs


  def read_config(path):
      with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
          return handle.read()


  def encoding_name():
      return codecs.lookup("utf-8").name
  ```

### Fix

No fix is offered when:

- no encoding is given, or it is `None`: `codecs.open()` then returns the builtin text file and ignores `errors`;

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import codecs


  def read_text(path):
      return codecs.open(path).read()
  ```

- the mode is not a string literal, or it has a `b`: a binary mode with an encoding returns a stream that `open()`
  rejects;

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import codecs


  def read_bytes(path):
      return codecs.open(path, "rb", "utf-8").read()
  ```

- a Ruff rule the project enables still flags the new `open()` call after Ruff's own fixes, such as PTH123
  (`builtin-open`) under the default settings, so simplint withdraws the fix;

- an argument is unpacked with `*` or `**`, or `open` is bound in the module, which the new call would pick up;

- the call has a comment inside it, which the rewrite would drop.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.10"
  ```

  ```python report
  import codecs


  def read_config(path):
      return codecs.open(
          path,  # the config file
          "r",
          "utf-8",
      ).read()
  ```

name: up-argparse-suggest-on-error
summary: `suggest_on_error=True` in `ArgumentParser()` calls
explanation:
Flags `suggest_on_error=True` in `argparse.ArgumentParser()` calls, which Python 3.15 makes the default.

## Why is this bad?

From Python 3.15 `argparse` suggests the closest valid choice on a mistyped argument without asking, so
`suggest_on_error=True` repeats the default. Before Python 3.14 the keyword does not exist at all, so the call fails
there with `TypeError`.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool", suggest_on_error=True)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool")
```

## Configuration

- [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and
  [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to
  [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python);
  see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version)

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff]
  target-version = "py315"
  ```

  ```python report
  import argparse

  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool", suggest_on_error=True)
  ```

## What it does

### Active on

- **`suggest_on_error=True` in calls of `argparse.ArgumentParser`**, by its qualified name or by a name imported from
  `argparse`. **Safe fix:** the keyword is removed with the comma that separates it from its neighbor.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python report
  import argparse

  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool", suggest_on_error=True)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import argparse

  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool")
  ```

### Exceptions

- **`suggest_on_error=False`**: it turns the suggestions off, which the default no longer does.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import argparse

  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool", suggest_on_error=False)
  ```

- **A value that is not the literal `True`**, such as `suggest_on_error=verbose`: its value is not known.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.15"
  ```

  ```python ok
  import argparse

  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tool", suggest_on_error=verbose)
  ```

### Fix

No fix is offered when the call has a comment, which the removal would drop. The keyword is still reported.

```toml config
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.15"
```

```python report
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    prog="tool",  # the CLI name
    suggest_on_error=True,
)
```
